seasons.caption: Meteosat satellite image at the March equinox: the terminator runs nearly pole to pole, as in the model when neither hemisphere tilts toward the Sun.

rotation.caption: Meteosat satellite image showing the day–night terminator. Earth's eastward rotation carries every place across this boundary at sunrise and sunset.
The historic Greenwich Meridian marker. Longitude is measured from here, and every 15° of longitude is about one hour of solar time.
Landsat image of the Diomede Islands, either side of the International Date Line: a convention where the calendar date changes, not a physical line.

moon-phases.caption: A first-quarter Moon: half the visible disc is lit when the Moon is about 90° from the Sun in our sky, as in the model's quarter position.
A nearly full Moon, lit almost completely because it lies roughly opposite the Sun. Earth's shadow does not cause the phase.

earth-interior.caption: The Kola Superdeep Borehole site. At 12.262 km it is the deepest hole ever drilled, yet it did not get through the continental crust.

Maps of magnetic-field strength at Earth's surface in 2014 and 2025, modeled from Swarm satellite measurements (colors show nanotesla). The field is generated mainly by moving liquid iron in the outer core, not by a permanent bar magnet.
A seismograph records ground motion as a wiggly line. P- and S-wave arrival times recorded around the world are the main evidence for the layers in the model.

plate-boundaries.caption: The San Andreas Fault, California: a transform boundary where the plates slide past each other horizontally.
The Himalaya from the ISS: a convergent boundary where continental crust has been shortened and thickened in a collision.

NOAA seafloor relief of the Puerto Rico Trench, where the North American Plate meets the Caribbean Plate at an oblique convergent boundary. Colors show measured depth with vertical relief exaggerated; the labels and boundary lines are added interpretation.

contours.caption: The Vale of Edale and Lose Hill, Peak District. Compare the real valley and spur shapes with the contour patterns the model draws.
A USGS topographic sheet of Yosemite Creek. Tightly packed contours mark steep valley sides; widely spaced ones mark gentle ground.

rivers.caption: A waterfall and plunge pool at Cwmorthin, Wales: a steep step typical of an upper course, where the long profile is steepest.
The Mississippi at Hannibal, Missouri: a wide lowland river on a gentle gradient, bordered by an engineered levee.
False-color Landsat image of the Lena Delta, Russia, where the river reaches base level and deposits its load.

water-cycle.caption: Forest canopy in Cameroon. Leaves intercept rainfall and return water to the air by transpiration.
Snowmelt feeding a stream in Idaho: water released from a snow store into surface flow.
A groundwater hand pump in India. Abstraction removes water from the groundwater store.

solar-system.caption: NASA MESSENGER mosaic of Mercury, a small rocky terrestrial planet close to the Sun.
Voyager 2 image of Neptune, an ice giant about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth. Its displayed color has been processed.
Earth photographed by Apollo 17: the largest of the four rocky terrestrial planets.

sun-earth.caption: NASA SDO view of the photosphere with a large sunspot group: the visible surface that supplies the sunlight in the model.
Meteosat satellite image at the December solstice. Sunlight strikes the southern hemisphere more directly, so equal beams spread over smaller areas there.

universe-scale.caption: Stars and nebulae in Orion. Stars that look close together in the sky can lie hundreds of light-years apart.
SDO image sequence of Venus crossing the Sun in 2012. Timing such transits helped astronomers measure the astronomical unit.

geologic-time.caption: A Middle Cambrian trilobite, roughly 500 million years old, from the Mount Stephen beds, Canada. Fossils mark positions on the timeline.
The K–Pg boundary at Trinidad Lake, Colorado, about 66 million years ago, when the non-bird dinosaurs disappeared.
The Grand Canyon exposes a long stack of rock layers, but unconformities mean parts of the record are missing.

eclipses.caption: A total lunar eclipse in January 2000. The Moon lies in Earth's umbra and is lit only by reddened light refracted through Earth's atmosphere.
Venus crossing the Sun in 2012. Like an eclipse, a transit needs the bodies to line up near an orbital node.

tides.caption: A first-quarter Moon. With the Sun and Moon at right angles, their tidal effects partly cancel, favoring neap tides.
A nearly full Moon. Near full and new Moon the Sun and Moon line up, favoring spring tides with a larger range.

solar-altitude.caption: Meteosat satellite image at the December solstice. The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, so northern noon altitudes are at their lowest.
Meteosat satellite image at the March equinox. The Sun is overhead at the equator, and the noon altitude at any latitude is 90° minus the latitude.

continental-drift.caption: A Glossopteris leaf fossil from Antarctica. The same plant fossils on separate southern continents suggest they were once joined in Pangaea.
NOAA bathymetry of the South Atlantic. The continental shelves of South America and Africa fit together closely, like the model's shelf fit.

hotspots.caption: Grand Prismatic Spring, Yellowstone: hydrothermal activity above a continental hotspot, inside the North American Plate.

NOAA multibeam survey of an Arctic seamount, shown in 3D with colors for depth; the vertical scale is probably exaggerated. Volcanoes carried away from a hotspot can cool and sink to become seamounts, although not every seamount forms this way.
A lava fountain on Kīlauea, 1983: the active volcanic end of the Hawaiian hotspot chain.

seafloor-spreading.caption: NOAA EMAG2 magnetic-anomaly map. Bands that run parallel to the mid-ocean ridges record reversals of Earth's magnetic field.
NOAA bathymetry of the South Atlantic, showing the Mid-Atlantic Ridge running midway between the continents.
Þingvellir, Iceland: a place where the spreading Mid-Atlantic Ridge rises above sea level and faults open the ground.

atmosphere-layers.caption: A radiosonde sounding from Lake Charles, Louisiana. Weather balloons measure temperature with height, giving the profile the model uses to define the layers.
NASA map of the Antarctic ozone hole, September 2023. The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere.
An aurora seen from the ISS, which itself orbits within the thermosphere. The green light is emitted by oxygen roughly 100–250 km above the surface.

energy-budget.caption: NASA CERES satellite map of reflected sunlight, 2000–2015 average: shortwave energy that clouds, ice and bright surfaces send back to space.
NASA CERES satellite map of outgoing longwave radiation: the infrared energy that Earth emits to space.
Snow and dark ground in the Cairngorms: a real high- and low-albedo contrast like the model's surface choices.

thermal-circulation.caption: GOES-19 satellite image: a cloud-free band beside Lake Michigan marks a land breeze, the night-time reversal of the sea breeze.
ECOSTRESS thermal map of London at night. Built-up areas stay warmer than green spaces: an urban heat island.
Southsea beach, Portsmouth. On sunny days the land warms faster than the sea, the contrast that drives a sea breeze.

wind.caption: A US National Weather Service surface chart. Closely spaced isobars mark a strong pressure gradient and strong winds.
MODIS satellite image of a depression northeast of Japan. Clouds spiral counterclockwise around the low, as Coriolis deflection predicts in the Northern Hemisphere.

three-cell.caption: MODIS satellite image of Hawaiʻi. Northeasterly trade winds, the surface branch of the Hadley cell, bring rain to windward slopes.
The Namib Desert: a subtropical desert beneath sinking air in the descending branch of the Hadley circulation, here combined with a cold offshore current.

fronts.caption: A US National Weather Service surface chart with cold, warm and occluded fronts drawn between air masses as a storm develops.
MODIS satellite image of a midlatitude depression. Long cloud bands mark the fronts wrapping around the low.

cyclone-anticyclone.caption: A US National Weather Service surface chart marking H and L pressure centers. Winds blow counterclockwise around lows in the Northern Hemisphere.
MODIS satellite image of Cyclone Evan near Fiji, in the Southern Hemisphere, where cyclones spiral clockwise.

climate-types.caption: Tropical rainforest in Cameroon: a landscape example of an Af (tropical wet) climate.
Namib Desert dunes: a landscape example of a hot desert (BW) climate.
Exmoor, North Devon: a landscape in the Cfb (temperate oceanic) climate.

drainage-basin.caption: The Moselle joins the Rhine at Koblenz, Germany: a confluence, where a tributary meets the main river.
Snowmelt streams near a source area in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains, high in a drainage basin.
False-color Landsat image of the Lena Delta, Russia: the river's mouth, where water from its basin reaches the Arctic Ocean.

hydrograph.caption: The Stillaguamish River in flood. Overbank water like this happens near the peak of a storm hydrograph.
Floodwater around Burrowbridge, Somerset, February 2014. Flat, saturated land produces a long, slow falling limb.

river-hydrology.caption: Snowmelt in Idaho's Sawtooth Mountains. Nival regimes peak when stored snow melts in spring and early summer.
Glen Canyon Dam, Arizona. Reservoir releases smooth the natural seasonal regime of the Colorado River downstream.

A USGS stream gauge at Huey Creek, Antarctica. Fed by glacier meltwater, the stream flows only for a few weeks in the southern summer. Records of stage and discharge reveal this strongly seasonal regime.

ocean-currents.caption: MODIS satellite image off Mauritania. The Canary Current, an eastern boundary current, is linked to upwelling of nutrient-rich water here.
Aquarius satellite salinity map. The saltiest surface water lies in the subtropical gyres, beneath the subtropical highs where evaporation exceeds rainfall.

thermohaline.caption: A NOAA CTD rosette measures temperature and salinity with depth, which together set seawater density.
Aquarius satellite map of sea-surface salinity, one of the two controls on density in the model.
A Deep SOLO float being deployed. Such floats measure temperature and salinity down to great depth, tracking deep-water masses.

carbon-cycle.caption: Leaf litter in New South Wales. Decomposers respire, returning carbon from the litter to the air: part of the fast carbon cycle.
A coal seam in Ohio. Burning this fossil fuel releases carbon stored for about 300 million years in the slow cycle.
Viru Bog, Estonia. Waterlogged peat stores carbon because decomposition is very slow.

enso.caption: Sentinel-6 satellite map of sea-surface height in January 2025: lower sea levels in the cool central and eastern Pacific during La Niña.

AMSR-E map of sea-surface temperature anomalies, 19 October 2004. Blue water was cooler than average and orange warmer. The warm pool north of Australia still held some of the warmest water on Earth; it was simply less warm than usual. Alt text: 'Global AMSR-E map of sea-surface temperature anomalies, blue where cooler than average and orange where warmer.'

landform-types.caption: The Himalaya from the ISS: mountains with very high elevation and relief.
The Ahuriri River plain, New Zealand: low relief and gentle slopes across a broad valley floor.
Makhtesh Ramon, Israel: an erosional basin enclosed by higher ground.

river-erosion.caption: Cwmorthin, Wales: a waterfall over a nick point with a plunge pool eroded below it.
Wutach Gorge, Germany: a narrow gorge cut by rapid downcutting.
New River Gorge, West Virginia: steep slopes falling to the river form a V-shaped valley.

river-deposition.caption: The Ucayali River, Peru, from the ISS. Meanders build slip-off slopes on inner bends while cut banks erode the outer bends.
An engineered levee on the Mississippi. Natural levées form where floodwater drops sediment beside the channel; this one is built.
Landsat image of the Thames estuary. Pale water carries suspended sediment that settles where the flow slows.

river-capture.caption: The Aitrach valley, Germany: a beheaded stream now far too small for the valley left after the Wutach captured its headwaters.

coasts.caption: Hvítserkur, Iceland: a sea stack with arches eroded through its base.
Chalk cliffs and offshore remnants in Purbeck, Dorset: stacks and stumps left as the cliff retreats.
A groyne at Tallebudgera Creek, Australia, interrupting longshore drift.

glaciers.caption: Yosemite Valley: a U-shaped trough, with Bridalveil Fall dropping from a hanging valley on the right.
Little Matterhorn, Montana: a pyramidal horn left by glacial erosion on several sides.
Aerial view of drumlins near Horicon Marsh, Wisconsin, streamlined by former ice flow.

karst.caption: Bimmah sinkhole, Oman: a doline formed by dissolution and collapse.
Broadway passage, Mammoth Cave, Kentucky: a large passage enlarged by groundwater dissolving limestone.

folds-faults.caption: The Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag, Scotland: a low-angle reverse fault (a thrust). The hanging wall above the fault plane carries older rocks over the younger footwall rocks below, recording compression.
Wallace Creek, California: the stream channel is offset sideways where it crosses the San Andreas, a strike-slip fault.
Þingvellir, Iceland: normal faults bound the rift where the crust is being stretched.

aeolian.caption: Yardangs at Dunhuang, China: streamlined ridges carved by wind abrasion.
A nabkha in the Mojave Desert: sand trapped around a mesquite shrub.
A 1930s Dust Bowl storm in Texas: deflation lifting fine soil into suspension.

rock-cycle.caption: Pillow lava at the Galápagos Rift: igneous rock formed as lava cools in seawater.
The Grand Canyon's layered cliffs: sedimentary rocks formed by deposition and lithification.
Weathered granite breaking down into loose material: the first step toward new sediment.

soil-profile.caption: A podzolic soil in Karelia. A thin pale gray E horizon lies just below the dark topsoil, above a rusty-brown B horizon. The paler sand near the bottom is the parent material.
A deep red Oxisol in Puerto Rico, formed by long, intense tropical weathering.
A Mollisol near Ponce, Puerto Rico, with a dark organic-rich A horizon over pale carbonate-rich subsoil.

soil-texture.caption: Kaolinite, a clay mineral. Clay as a texture class means particles smaller than 0.002 mm, whatever the mineral.
Iowa's Loess Hills are made of silt-rich wind-blown sediment, which would plot near the silt corner of the texture triangle.

weathering.caption: Angular blocks on Foel Fras, Wales: mechanical weathering, such as frost shattering, breaks rock without changing its minerals.
Limestone pavement at Malham: carbonation, a type of chemical weathering, has dissolved the joints into grykes.

soil-erosion.caption: A raindrop hitting bare soil (USDA NRCS): rain splash detaches particles before runoff moves them.
Loess hills in Shanxi, China, deeply cut by gullies where concentrated runoff erodes soft silt.
A Dust Bowl dust storm in Texas: wind erosion of bare, dry soil.

earthquakes.caption: USGS ShakeMap of the 2021 Haiti earthquake. The star marks the epicenter and the colored rings show intensity falling with distance.
A seismograph drum records the shaking as a line on paper. The arrival times of P-, S- and surface waves are used to locate the focus.

volcanoes.caption: Mount Fuji, Japan: a steep-sided stratovolcano built from layers of lava and fragmental deposits.
Pyroclastic-flow deposits filling a valley below Pinatubo after its 1991 eruption.
A fissure eruption on Kīlauea, 2011: runny basaltic lava erupting along a linear crack.

tsunami.caption: NASA ARIA satellite map of ground displacement after the 2025 Kamchatka megathrust earthquake. This kind of sudden seabed movement can trigger a tsunami.
A wind wave breaking in Portugal, for contrast. Its wavelength is tens of meters; a tsunami's can be hundreds of kilometers.

tropical-cyclone.caption: Satellite image of Typhoon Mangkhut, 2018, with a compact eye and spiral rainbands.
MODIS satellite image of Cyclone Evan near Fiji: a Southern Hemisphere tropical cyclone spiraling clockwise.
New Orleans flooded after Hurricane Katrina, 2005: storm surge and failed defenses caused much of the damage.

graticule.caption: A Mollweide world map with the graticule drawn: meridians converge at the poles, while parallels never meet.
The Diomede Islands, either side of the International Date Line, which roughly follows the 180° meridian.
NASA Blue Marble on an equirectangular latitude–longitude grid. No lines are drawn here, but on this projection every meridian and parallel would plot as an evenly spaced straight line.

map-projections.caption: The Mercator projection keeps local angles but greatly enlarges high latitudes.
The Mollweide projection keeps relative areas correct but distorts shapes near its edges.
Globe gores from 1615: tapering strips that could be pasted on to a sphere with little distortion.

grid-references.caption: A USGS US Topo map with its 1 km UTM grid. Read the principal digits along the edges: eastings along the top and bottom first, then northings up the sides.
An older USGS topographic sheet of Yosemite Creek. Its red numbered squares are Public Land Survey System sections (township and range), not UTM grid squares: always check which grid a map uses.
An Ordnance Survey sheet of northeast Scotland. The British National Grid works the same way as the US National Grid, but a two-letter code (here NO) names each 100 km square.
The Greenwich Meridian marker. WGS84 GPS longitude differs from this historic line by about 102 meters, a reminder that coordinate systems differ.

mass-movement.caption: Rotational slumping above Redcliff Point, Dorset: blocks slide and tilt on a curved shear surface.

rain-shadow.caption: A föhn cloud wall over a ridge on Réunion: moist air rises and cools on the windward side, then sinks and warms on the lee side.
Fog and cloud on the Blue Mountains of Jamaica, where moist air forced up over high ground produces orographic cloud and rain.

groundwater.caption: A USGS observation well in Georgia that records changes in the water table.
A hand pump in India. Pumping abstracts groundwater and can create a cone of depression around the well.
London Clay at Walton-on-the-Naze, Essex: a low-permeability layer that can act as an aquitard.

isostasy.caption: The Himalaya from the ISS. High mountains are supported by a deep root of thickened crust, as in the model.
The Aletsch Glacier, Switzerland. Ice sheets far thicker than this pressed the crust down, and it rebounds when the ice melts.

wilson-cycle.caption: The Moine Thrust at Knockan Crag, Scotland: a record of Caledonian collision when the Iapetus Ocean closed.
MODIS satellite image of the Appalachian ridges, folded during continental collisions that assembled Pangaea.
NOAA bathymetry of the South Atlantic: passive margins on both sides of an ocean that opened as Africa and South America rifted apart.

soil-catena.caption: Gley clay compared with oxidized clay. Waterlogged soils at the foot of a slope often become gray gleys.
A thin ranker soil over granite in Brittany, typical of steep upper slopes where soil stays shallow.
A Puerto Rico soil whose parent material includes colluvium, sediment moved downslope and deposited.

periglacial.caption: A blockfield on Foel Fras, Wales, broken up by frost shattering in past periglacial conditions.

storm-surge.caption: New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina, 2005: low-lying neighborhoods flooded after the surge and the failure of flood defenses.
The Thames Barrier, London. Its gates close to keep tidal surges out of the upper estuary.

Landsat image of the northern Gulf coast (colors enhanced). The faint, broken arc at lower left is Louisiana's Chandeleur Islands, which storm surges and waves repeatedly overwash and break up. The brighter islands across the top lie off Mississippi and Alabama.
